Filtration. A physical or mechanical laboratory operation used to separate solid particles from a fluid, whether liquid or gas, by passing the mixture through a porous medium. The solid residue is retained on the filter medium, while the purified fluid, known as the filtrate, passes through. It is a fundamental technique for isolation, purification, and waste treatment.

The simplest form is gravity filtration, used for simple separations where a mixture is poured through a fluted filter paper in a funnel, relying solely on gravity to separate the phases. For more rapid isolation of recrystallized solids, vacuum filtration, also called suction filtration, utilizes a Büchner or Hirsch funnel, a vacuum flask, and a water aspirator or pump. When handling highly reactive or corrosive solvents that would dissolve or react with standard paper filters, fritted glass funnels, also called sintered glass, are employed.

During recrystallization, cold filtration is used to remove insoluble impurities from a hot solution before crystallization of the target compound begins. Membrane filters with tiny, calibrated pore sizes such as zero point two-two micrometers sterilize heat-sensitive liquid media by physically trapping bacteria and other microbes. Municipal water treatment plants rely on sand and carbon filtration to remove particulate matter and impurities. Filtration serves as a peer separation technique that uses a porous barrier instead of rapid spinning to separate solids from liquids, and it requires a two-step process during recrystallization: hot gravity filtration to remove insoluble impurities, and cold vacuum filtration to collect the final crystals.
